scenario: You're filling up at a gas station during a long power outage. A car pulls in with four people who look at you, then at the supplies in your truck bed, then talk quietly to each other. Your tank is half full and you're 30 feet from your truck. What is the best next move?

options.text: Keep pumping and watch them closely until you're sure what they want
Stop pumping, get in your truck, lock the doors, and drive to a busier, staffed place - half a tank is enough for now
Walk over and ask them directly what they're looking at
Stand in front of your truck bed to show them you're guarding it

explanation: Several warning signs together - attention on you and your supplies, then quiet coordination - are your cue to act early while leaving is still easy. Getting into your locked vehicle and going somewhere busy costs you a few minutes of fuel time. Waiting to be sure (a) gives up your head start. Confronting them (c) or posturing (d) can escalate a situation that may have been nothing. Next time, cover supplies so they aren't on display.

scenario: A week-long power outage is forecast for your area and you have one weekend to improve your home's security. Rank these tasks from highest to lowest priority.

items.text: Replace short strike-plate screws with 3-4 inch screws and make sure every exterior door has a working deadbolt
Trim shrubs near doors and windows to about 2 feet so neighbors can see your entrances
Install solar or battery motion lights at the side and back entrances
Trade phone numbers with neighbors and agree on a group text or radio channel
Add battery door and window alarms

explanation: Solid, locked doors come first - most break-ins go through doors, and a stronger strike plate is cheap and fast. Neighbors are next: people who watch out for each other give the best early warning and help in a long outage. Motion lights that work without grid power remove dark approaches. Trimming shrubs improves sightlines but matters a bit less in a short outage. Alarms are useful extras once the basics are done. Never add traps or anything meant to injure - they're illegal and hurt the wrong people.

scenario: Two days after a flood, a man in a FEMA shirt knocks on your door. He says he can 'fast-track' your disaster grant today if you pay a $200 processing fee and give him your bank account number. What should you do?

options.text: Pay the fee but ask for a receipt
Give him the bank number but not the fee, since FEMA deposits grants directly
Decline, ask to see a laminated photo ID badge, and call the FEMA Helpline (800-621-3362) to verify - then report him to the fraud hotline and police
Let him in to inspect the damage since the shirt shows he's official

explanation: FEMA never charges for inspections or help, and real disaster workers never accept money. A FEMA shirt is not proof - real staff carry a laminated photo ID badge. Verify any contact through the FEMA Helpline, and report fraud to 866-720-5721 or ReportFraud.ftc.gov and local police. Giving bank details (b) or a receipt for a fake fee (a) still hands a scammer what they want.

scenario: After a hurricane, a roofer stops by and offers a great price - but only if you sign today and pay half up front in cash so he can 'buy materials before prices go up.' You do need a new roof. What's the best response?

options.text: Accept - prices really do rise after storms and he seems honest
Pay by payment app instead of cash so there's a record

Decline the same-day deal; check his license with your state or county, ask for proof of insurance, get written estimates and a contract, and pay by credit card with the balance due only when the work is done
Sign the contract but tell him you'll pay the deposit tomorrow

explanation: The FTC advises using only licensed and insured contractors, getting a written contract, avoiding cash, and paying in full only after the work is finished. Pressure to sign today and pay cash up front are classic red flags. Payment apps (b) are hard to reverse, much like cash. Signing first (d) can lock you into a bad deal.

scenario: You're in a large store when you hear gunshots from the front entrance. The back stockroom door is about 50 feet away and the path to it is clear. Put these actions in the order you should do them.

items.text: Leave your cart and go out the back door, urging people near you to come
Keep moving away from the building and warn others not to go in
Call 911 and tell them where the shooting is and what you saw
When police arrive, keep your hands empty and visible and follow their commands

explanation: With a clear path out, RUN is the best option: leave belongings and go immediately. Keep putting distance between you and the danger and stop others from walking in. Call 911 as soon as you are safely away - do not assume someone else called. When officers arrive, show empty hands and follow commands, because they do not yet know who the attacker is. Hiding or fighting are only for when you cannot get out.

scenario: Your nephew, age 8, is staying with you during a power outage. You own a handgun and usually keep it in your nightstand drawer. What is the safest way to store it while he's there?

options.text: Leave it in the nightstand but tell him the room is off-limits
Hide it on a high closet shelf where he can't reach
Unload it and lock it in a safe or lockbox, lock the ammunition separately, keep the key or code away from him, and teach him to stop, not touch, leave, and tell an adult if he ever sees a gun
Keep it loaded but put a trigger lock on it

explanation: Children find hidden guns, and rules alone don't stop curious kids. Safe storage means unloaded, locked in a safe or lockbox, with ammunition locked separately and keys or codes out of reach. A lock on a loaded gun (d) is weaker than locked, unloaded storage. Teaching the stop-don't touch-leave-tell rule adds another layer. Many states also have child access laws, so follow yours.

scenario: You're volunteering at a water distribution table. A man who has waited three hours learns the truck is out of gallon jugs. He starts shouting, his face is red, and he steps toward the table. He has no weapon and hasn't threatened anyone. What's the best first response?

options.text: Tell him firmly to calm down or leave
Keep the table between you, keep your hands open and visible, speak slowly and quietly, acknowledge his long wait, and offer what you can - smaller bottles now or a time when more jugs arrive
Explain the logistics problem in detail so he understands it isn't your fault
Walk around the table and put a hand on his shoulder to reassure him

explanation: CISA's de-escalation guidance stresses distance, open and visible hands, a calm slow voice, and active listening. Acknowledging his frustration and offering realistic options helps him regain control. Saying 'calm down' (a) usually inflames people, a detailed argument (c) feels dismissive, and touching an agitated person (d) can trigger violence. If he threatens anyone or reaches for a weapon, step away and call 911.

scenario: Your house has tall hedges in front of the windows for privacy, a dark side yard, and house numbers hidden by a vine. Based on crime prevention through environmental design (CPTED), which change helps the most?

options.text: Let the hedges grow even taller so no one can see in
Trim shrubs to about 2 feet and tree limbs up to about 6 feet, add motion lights to the side yard, and make house numbers visible
Put up a sign saying the house is guarded
Paint the windows over so valuables can't be seen

explanation: CPTED relies on natural surveillance: tall hedges block neighbors' view and give someone a hiding place right at your windows. Trimming shrubs to about 2 feet and limbs up to about 6 feet, lighting dark areas, and showing your house numbers make your home visible and easier for responders to find. Painting windows (d) blocks fire escape and your own view; keep valuables out of sight instead.

scenario: You're returning home after a wildfire evacuation. At night, you reach a re-entry checkpoint staffed by deputies and National Guard. Your driver's license shows your old address. What should you do?

options.text: Drive around the cones on the shoulder since you live there
Slow down, turn on your interior light, keep your hands on the wheel, tell the officer before reaching for anything, and show your license plus a utility bill or lease with your current address
Insist loudly that it's your right to go home and refuse to show anything
Give a neighbor's address that matches your license

explanation: Checkpoints control access to areas that may still be dangerous, and the supervisor decides who enters. Calm, visible hands and saying what you're reaching for keep the stop safe. Carry a photo ID plus proof of residence such as a utility bill, lease, or deed if your ID shows another address. Going around (a) is dangerous and illegal, arguing (c) won't change the decision, and false information (d) can lead to arrest. If you're turned away, leave by the route directed.

scenario: Your wallet, with your Social Security card and debit card, was lost during an evacuation. You want to stop anyone from opening new credit in your name, and you also want to keep things simple while you're living out of a shelter. Which statement is correct?

options.text: A credit freeze costs about $10 per bureau and expires after 90 days
A fraud alert is free, lasts one year, and you only need to contact one bureau; a credit freeze is also free but must be placed with each of the three bureaus
You must file a police report before any credit bureau will place a fraud alert
Only a paid identity-protection service can freeze your credit

explanation: Under federal law since 2018, both fraud alerts and credit freezes are free. A fraud alert lasts one year and one bureau must notify the other two. A freeze is stronger, lasts until you lift it, and must be placed with Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion separately. Also call your bank to cancel the debit card, check reports at annualcreditreport.com, and use IdentityTheft.gov if fraud appears.

start.scenario: It's been 72 hours since a widespread grid failure. No power, spotty phones, low water pressure in your suburban neighborhood. Your home is undamaged. You have about 30 days of food, 50 gallons of water, a car with 3/4 tank of fuel, and relatives 180 miles away. Officials have not ordered an evacuation. A group of strangers has been hanging around the neighborhood entrance. What do you do?

options.text: Leave tonight for your relatives' place before things get worse
Stay home for now, keep monitoring official updates, and set clear triggers for when you would leave

leave_night.scenario: You leave after dark. Forty miles out, the highway is jammed with stalled and abandoned cars and a bridge is closed. Your fuel gauge drops as you idle. What now?

options.text: Abandon the car and walk the remaining 140 miles
Turn back home on a known road while you still have fuel, and contact your relatives when you can

foot_march.explanation: Walking 140 miles with what you can carry, away from your supplies and shelter, is extremely risky. Leaving at night with no evacuation order and an undamaged home traded safety for uncertainty. Evacuate early when officials order it or when a real hazard threatens your home, travel in daylight, and plan backup routes and fuel. If your plan can only work by walking a long distance, it isn't a safe plan.

return_home.explanation: Good recovery. You recognized the plan had failed and returned to your supplies and shelter while you still had fuel. The lesson: with an undamaged home, supplies, and no evacuation order, staying put was the stronger choice. Leave when officials order it or a hazard threatens you, go in daylight, and have more than one route.

shelter_in_place.scenario: Day 4: the group at the entrance has grown and police have been seen talking with them. Day 7: two homes on your street are broken into. Neighbors invite you to join a mutual-aid group that checks on each other and runs a watch from members' porches. What do you do?

options.text: Join - share contact info and help with the watch, but don't list your full supplies
Stay to yourself - telling anyone anything could make you a target

mutual_aid.explanation: Neighbors who look out for each other spot fires, medical emergencies, and break-ins early and call for help faster. You can join without revealing your inventory - offer time and skills, and keep a small 'sharing' supply. Keep the watch to observing and reporting from members' own property, never confronting anyone, and report break-ins to police.

opsec_solo.explanation: Privacy about supplies is smart, but total isolation leaves you without early warning or help. No single household can stay alert around the clock for weeks. Joining a neighborhood group while keeping your inventory private is the better balance.

start.scenario: Day 10 of a regional disaster. You're at your rural home with your family. Three tired-looking adults with light packs walk up your driveway and stop at the gate. One waves in a friendly way. What do you do?

options.text: Stay inside with the door locked and talk to them through a window or door from a safe spot
Walk out alone to the gate to see what they want

talk_safely.scenario: Speaking calmly through the window, you learn they walked from a city 60 miles away looking for water and food. They say a 10-year-old is waiting on the road. What do you do?

options.text: Invite them all inside to rest - a family with a child is surely harmless
Set out water and some food at the gate, tell them where the nearest official shelter or aid point is, and keep the door locked

gate_aid.explanation: You helped people in need while keeping your family safe. Staying inside, speaking calmly, and leaving water at the gate meets an urgent need without opening your home to strangers. Pointing them to a shelter or aid site gets them longer-term help. If anything about the situation changes or feels threatening, lock up and call 911.

inside_too_fast.explanation: Kindness is good, but inviting strangers into your home during a crisis puts your family at risk, whatever their appearance. You can be generous from behind a locked door: leave water and food at the gate and direct them to official shelters, where staff can help them safely.

approach_gate.explanation: Walking out alone puts you in the open, away from your family and your phone, with no easy retreat. You can have the same conversation through a door or window. Stay inside, keep it locked, speak calmly, and call 911 if anyone becomes threatening.
